---
title: "SVG elements are DOM objects too"
---

Every shape in your drawings so far was typed by hand into `index.html`. A
chart with twelve bars, or a canvas that fills up while the user clicks,
cannot work that way. The program has to build the shapes, the same way your
code built list items in Part 2: create an element, set what it needs, append
it. The first of those three steps has a trap in it, so walk into the trap
once and you will recognize it forever.

## A circle that stays invisible {#sec-svg-dom-experiment}

1. Create a new app from the
   [vite-ts-starter](https://github.com/Teaching-HTL-Leonding/vite-ts-starter)
   template inside `coursework/` of your course repository, run `npm install`.
2. In `index.html`, replace everything between `<body>` and `</body>` with
   this:

   ```html
   <h1>Shapes from code</h1>
   <svg id="canvas" viewBox="0 0 400 300" width="400" role="img" aria-label="Drawing area"></svg>
   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

   The `role` and `aria-label` give the drawing a name for a screen reader.
   Biome's accessibility rule asks every `<svg>` for such a name, so put the
   pair on every drawing you make.

3. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with this:

   ```ts
   const canvas = document.querySelector<SVGSVGElement>('#canvas');
   if (!canvas) {
     throw new Error('No element with the id canvas');
   }

   const circle = document.createElement('circle');
   circle.setAttribute('cx', '100');
   circle.setAttribute('cy', '80');
   circle.setAttribute('r', '40');
   circle.setAttribute('fill', 'crimson');
   canvas.append(circle);

   console.log(circle.constructor.name);
   ```

4. Run `npm start`.

The page shows the heading and nothing else. No red circle, and no complaint
in the console either. Press F12 and look in the **Elements** tab: the line
`<circle cx="100" cy="80" r="40" fill="crimson"></circle>` sits inside the
`<svg>`, spelled exactly as you meant it. In the **Console** tab your log line
reads `HTMLUnknownElement`.

That name is the whole story. Now put this line above the `createElement` call
and change `createElement` to `createElementNS`:

```ts
const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';
const circle = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'circle');
```

Save. The circle appears, and the console now says `SVGCircleElement`.

## Two dictionaries, one page {#sec-svg-dom-namespace}

HTML and SVG were invented by different groups, and their tag names overlap.
Both have an `a` and both have a `title`, and the two `title` tags mean
different things. So every tag name belongs to a **namespace**, which
is the dictionary its name is looked up in. The SVG dictionary is named by the
address in `SVG_NS`, and that address is a name, not a page your browser
downloads.

When the browser parses your `index.html` and reaches `<svg>`, it switches
dictionaries for everything inside, which is why the shapes you wrote by hand
in the previous chapter simply worked. `document.createElement` never switches.
It always looks the name up in the HTML dictionary, and HTML has no `circle`,
so the browser hands back an object of the type `HTMLUnknownElement`. That is a
real element which keeps its attributes and sits in the tree, and which the
browser never draws.

`document.createElementNS` takes the dictionary as its first argument. Put
`const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';` at the top of every file that
builds SVG, and use it for every shape you create.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Shapes in DevTools all look right

A wrong-namespace `circle` and a correct one are printed the same way in the
Elements tab. When shapes refuse to appear, `createElement` instead of
`createElementNS` is the first suspect, and `console.log(shape.constructor.name)`
settles it in one reload.
:::

## Attributes, always as strings {#sec-svg-dom-attributes}

Everything about a shape is an attribute: `cx`, `cy`, and `r` on a circle,
`x`, `y`, `width`, and `height` on a rectangle, plus `fill`, `stroke`, and
`stroke-width` on both. You set all of them with `setAttribute`, and its second
argument is a string, so a number goes through `String()` on the way in:

```ts
const radius = 40;
circle.setAttribute('r', String(radius));
```

Forget the `String()` and TypeScript stops you with
`Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'`.

Do not go looking for a shortcut through properties. `circle.cx = 100` does not
compile, because `cx` is a read-only property holding an object that describes
the length together with its animated value. Every geometry value in this book
goes in through `setAttribute`.

## The type family grows {#sec-svg-dom-types}

You meet a new element type in almost every chapter, `HTMLButtonElement` for a
button and `HTMLInputElement` for an input. SVG continues the family the same
way, one type per tag: `SVGCircleElement`, `SVGRectElement`, and `SVGElement`
for all of them together. The `<svg>` tag itself is an `SVGSVGElement`, where
the doubled SVG is not a typo but the SVG element of the SVG family.

TypeScript knows the tag names, so `createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'rect')` hands back
an `SVGRectElement` without any help from you. Hover the variable in VS Code
and read what it says. For the element that is already in your HTML you name
the type yourself, exactly as you have done since Part 2:

```ts
const canvas = document.querySelector<SVGSVGElement>('#canvas');
```

## CSS reaches shapes too {#sec-svg-dom-css}

A shape carries classes like any other element, and `classList.add` and
`classList.toggle` work on it unchanged. What changes are the properties worth
setting. `color` and `background-color` do nothing to
a circle, because SVG paints the inside with `fill` and the outline with
`stroke`:

```css
.shape:hover {
  opacity: 0.7;
  cursor: pointer;
}

.selected {
  stroke: black;
  stroke-width: 4;
}
```

One rule about the two ways to set a color. A `fill` you set with
`setAttribute` loses against a `fill` in the stylesheet, always, no matter how
plain the selector is. Decide per property where it lives: the color a user
picks belongs on the element, and the look of a state such as `selected`
belongs in the stylesheet.

## Clicks land on the shape {#sec-svg-dom-clicks}

A shape is an event target like a button, so there is nothing new to learn:

```ts
circle.addEventListener('click', () => {
  circle.classList.toggle('selected');
});
```

A click on the circle also reaches a listener on the `<svg>` around it. Inside
either listener, `event.target` is the object the click actually landed on, so
`event.target === canvas` is how you ask whether the user hit empty space
rather than a shape.

## From the mouse to the drawing {#sec-svg-dom-mouse}

A `click` event carries `event.clientX` and `event.clientY`, which count from
the top left corner of the browser's content area, not from your drawing.
`canvas.getBoundingClientRect()` measures where the `<svg>` currently sits in
that same counting, and the difference between the two is the position inside
the drawing:

```ts
canvas.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const box = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
  const x = event.clientX - box.left;
  const y = event.clientY - box.top;
  console.log(`${x} / ${y}`);
});
```

Those two numbers are pixels on the screen, and the coordinates you feed into
`cx` and `cy` are viewBox units. They are the same numbers only while the
`<svg>` is as wide on screen as its `viewBox` says, which is why every drawing
in this chapter uses `width="400"` next to `viewBox="0 0 400 300"`. Keep that
pairing and the subtraction above is all the math you need.

::: {.research title="What is in that rectangle?"}
The exercise below picks random sizes for its shapes, and its bonus step turns
a click into a position inside the drawing. Both need something the chapter
did not spell out.

1. `getBoundingClientRect()` gives back one object full of numbers. Name four
   of its properties and say what each one measures.
2. Clicking a shape in the exercise removes it with `remove()`. What happens to
   the click listener that was attached to that element, and can the element
   come back into the page afterwards?
3. You need a whole random number between two bounds, for example a radius
   from 10 to 50 with both ends possible. Write the expression using
   `Math.random()` and `Math.floor()`, and say which part of it lets 50 come
   out.

Question 3 is exam material: random numbers in a range show up in almost every
drawing task, and the exam has no internet and no AI.
:::

## Exercise: shape generator {#sec-svg-dom-exercise}

A toolbar picks a kind of shape and a color, a button drops one onto the
canvas at a random spot, and clicking a shape takes it away again.

{{< exercise shape-generator >}}

1. Open `index.html` and read it: a toolbar with a `<select id="shapeKind">`,
   an `<input type="color" id="shapeColor">`, an **Add shape** button, a
   **Clear all** button, then the `<svg id="canvas">` with a `viewBox` of
   `0 0 600 400`, and a paragraph `<p id="shapeStatus">` under it.
2. In `src/index.ts`, import the stylesheet with `import './styles.css';` and
   put `const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';` under it. Look up the six
   elements with `querySelector<...>` and cover them with one `if` that throws.
   The steps below call them `canvas`, `shapeKind`, `shapeColor`, `addButton`,
   `clearButton`, and `shapeStatus`.
3. Write a helper `const randomBetween = (min: number, max: number) => { ... };`
   that returns a whole number from `min` to `max`, both included. The research
   box above has the expression.
4. Write a helper that adds one shape. When `shapeKind.value` is `'circle'`,
   create a `circle` with `createElementNS` and set `cx`, `cy`, and a random
   `r` between 10 and 50. Otherwise create a `rect` and set `x`, `y`, a random
   `width` between 20 and 100, and a random `height` between 20 and 80. Set
   `fill` to `shapeColor.value` in both cases. Remember `String()` around every
   number.
5. Give every new shape the class `shape` with `classList.add`, then append it
   to `canvas`. Expected result: nothing on screen yet, because no button calls
   your helper.
6. Listen for a click on `addButton` and call the helper with a random position
   inside the canvas, such as an `x` between 60 and 540 and a `y` between 60
   and 340. Expected result: every click drops a new shape of the chosen kind
   and color somewhere in the drawing.
7. Give each shape its own click listener that calls `remove()` on it. Expected
   result: clicking a shape takes it off the canvas, and the shapes around it
   stay where they are.
8. Listen for a click on `clearButton` and empty the drawing with
   `canvas.replaceChildren()`, which throws out every child of the `<svg>` in
   one call.
9. Keep the status line honest. Write a helper that reads
   `canvas.querySelectorAll('.shape').length` and writes a line such as
   `4 shapes on the canvas` into `shapeStatus`. Call it after adding, after
   removing, after clearing, and once at the end of the file so the page starts
   with `0 shapes on the canvas`.
10. Run `npm run check` and fix what Biome reports.
11. Bonus: make a click on empty canvas space add a shape right there. Put a
    click listener on `canvas`, leave the handler at once when
    `event.target !== canvas`, and otherwise turn `event.clientX` and
    `event.clientY` into a position with the subtraction from this chapter.
    Expected result: shapes appear under the mouse pointer, and clicking an
    existing shape still only removes it.

Test the whole thing once with both kinds and two colors, then clear the
canvas and watch the status line go back to zero.
